spec.name: Nostromo Galley
spec.description: A cutaway corner of a grimy 1979 commercial-tug galley: steel counters, range with hood, tall fridge and lockers, a bolted mess table with benches, exposed pipes and amber CRT glow.
spec.layout: A cutaway room module, 3.8 m wide (x) by 3.8 m long (z) by 2.6 m tall, viewed from the open front (+Z). The deck slab is y 0..0.08 and covers x ±1.9, z ±1.9. Two walls stand on it: the BACK bulkhead (inner face z = -1.8, outer face z = -1.9) and the RIGHT bulkhead (inner face x = -1.8, outer face x = -1.9). Both are 2.6 m tall. The LEFT side (+X) is open apart from a short end bulkhead with a round hatch doorway at x = 1.85 (z -0.5..0.8); the front stays open. Along the back wall runs the counter-and-range run (x -1.1..1.75, depth to z -1.1). Along the right wall runs the fridge and locker run (a tall fridge in the back corner, then base units and a dispenser out to z = 1.0, depth to x -1.1). A long bolted mess table with a bench on each side stands in the centre (table x ±0.55, z -0.7..0.9). Overhead sit a hood over the range, a pipe bundle, ceiling beams, lamp panels, a hanging utensil rail and a swing-arm CRT monitor. Style: everything is hard-edged boxes and cylinders in dull, dirty, lived-in industrial plastic and steel. The walls are faded beige-cream panels with dark ribbed seams, and every cabinet has rivet rows, recessed handles and scuffed darker strips at the kick plates. There are yellow/black hazard stripes, stencilled numbers and warning labels built as small thin boxes, orange and copper pipes, and chunky toggle switches. Each lived-in detail is its own thin part (grime streaks, rust patches, drips). Only the small lights and screens glow (amber, green CRT, cyan, red). Everything else stays matte. No curves beyond 8-12 segment cylinders.

parts.builds: The room enclosure and its dressing. The deck slab (deckGrey) y 0..0.08 over x ±1.9 and z ±1.9, with diamond-plate-style grating strips (grating, thin boxes in a grid) laid on the deck walkway between the table and the counters, and bolted floor plates with rivet heads. A yellow/black hazard stripe border (many alternating thin hazardYellow/hazardBlack slanted boxes) along the front edge of both counter runs and around the hatch. The back bulkhead and right bulkhead are built from tall wallBeige panels (about 0.6 m wide, 0.04 m thick) separated by wallDark vertical ribs and horizontal seam bars at y 0.95, 1.5 and 2.3. They carry rivet rows, hullGrey base skirting with a grime strip, a few rust and grime streak patches, stencilled number plates (small panelCream plates with dark thin bars as digits), warning label rectangles (hazardYellow with hazardBlack bars) and conduit runs (orangePipe and copper small tubes with clamps) running vertically near the corners. The left end bulkhead at x = 1.85 has a round hatch frame (octagonal ring of steelDark, with a wheel lock handle) and wall segments either side. Includes the wall light-switch panels and a few cable bundles (blackRubber) hanging along the walls. It builds NO furniture, counters, ceiling beams or lamps.
parts.attaches: Inner wall faces are the mounts backWallFace (z = -1.8) and rightWallFace (x = -1.8). The deck top (y = 0.08) is the mount deckTop that every other part stands on. The hatch is at leftHatch. Nothing from other parts should be built inside the wall thickness.

parts.builds: The counter run along the back wall, x -1.1..1.75, depth z -1.78..-1.1, standing on the deck at y 0.08 with its top at y 0.95. Base cabinets of steel (steel/steelDark) with recessed handle bars, rivet rows, door seams and a grime kick plate (blackRubber, 0.1 m high). A countertop slab (stainless) with a raised lip and scuff marks. Left part (x -1.1..-0.6): a prep counter holding a cutting board (panelCream), a knife block and a utensil pot. Sink (x -0.6..0.2, centred at sinkCentre): a double stainless basin with dark recesses, a swan-neck faucet in copper/steel with a handle, a drain grille and a dish rack with plates. Range (x 0.2..1.2, centred at rangeCentre): a stove with four burner rings (blackRubber rings, steelDark grates, small amber glowing indicator dots), a front control panel with five chunky knobs and tiny label strips, an oven door with a window (blackRubber with an amber glow strip) and a handle bar, plus a pot with a lid and a steaming kettle on the burners. Right part (x 1.2..1.75): a coffee machine (hullGrey body with a cyanLed glowing display, a red LED, a drip tray and a carafe), a stack of food trays, and a small microwave unit (panelCream with a dark window and a glowing timer digit panel in greenCRT). Shallow wall shelf blocks above are NOT included. The hood is built by the overhead part.
parts.attaches: Rests on deckTop. Back faces touch backWallFace (z = -1.8). The range centre is the mount rangeCentre, the sink the mount sinkCentre and the counter top the mount counterTop. Its x = -1.1 end meets the fridge's side at the back-right corner (the fridge body occupies x < -1.1).

parts.builds: The cold storage and locker run along the right wall (inner face x = -1.8), occupying x -1.78..-1.1. A tall fridge in the back corner (z -1.78..-1.1, height 2.0, centred at fridgeFront): a panelCream and hullGrey body with a two-door split (freezer on top), heavy vertical handle bars, a steel latch with a lever, hinge cylinders, a seal strip (blackRubber), a hazard label plate and a frost-blue recessed vent. A glowing cyanLed temperature display with a tiny digit block and a red LED. Then base units along the wall (z -1.1..1.0, top y 0.95, rightCounterTop): drawer fronts (steel) with recessed handles and rivet corners, a rounded-box trash compactor with a foot pedal and a warning label, a built-in drink and soup dispenser (hullGrey housing, 3 nozzles, a drip grille, a glowing amber display with a greenCRT cursor bar and push buttons), and a countertop set with a toaster, a stack of bowls (mugWhite), a canned goods stack (steel cans with foodRed and foodGreen label bands) and a bread box. A locker bank on the wall above the base units (y 1.25..2.0, z -1.0..0.9): five small steel hatch doors with latches, number stencils and an orangePipe strip. Everything stays at x < -1.1 on the room side and is flush against the wall at x = -1.8.
parts.attaches: Rests on deckTop. The back face touches rightWallFace (x = -1.8). The fridge corner shares the back-right corner with the back run's end at x = -1.1. The base units' top is the mount rightCounterTop.

parts.builds: The central mess table set and the two benches. The table (tableCentre, top at y 0.78) has a thick hullGrey top slab (x ±0.55, z -0.7..0.9) with a steel edge rim and rivet heads, a grime-worn scuffed centre strip and a hazard-yellow edge stripe at each end. Two chunky pedestal bases (steelDark, square, each with a bolted foot flange and floor bolts) at z -0.35 and z 0.55. Two bolted benches (x ±0.65..±0.95 around the table, seat height 0.46) with panelCream padded seats, blackRubber seat edge strips, steelDark legs with cross braces and foot plates. Tableware: six steel food trays with compartments (alternating foodGreen and foodRed blobs as flattened spheres and boxes), mugs (mugWhite cylinders with handle loops and a dark coffee disc on top), a water pitcher, salt and pepper shakers, a sauce bottle with a red cap, forks and spoons (thin steel boxes), a folded napkin, a dropped spoon, a half-eaten food tin with a lid, a handheld data-pad with a small greenCRT screen, and a smear of grime and a spilled drop (small flat discs). Items sit on the table top at y 0.78 or on the bench seats.
parts.attaches: Feet rest on deckTop. The table centre is the mount tableCentre, the bench seats are benchSeatL (x +0.8) and benchSeatR (x -0.8). It clears the back run (z < -1.1) and the right run (x < -1.1).

parts.builds: Everything hanging above y 1.45 plus wall-mounted fittings. The range hood above the range (x 0.2..1.2, z -1.78..-1.05, centred on hoodBase y 1.65..2.1): a tapered steel box with a dark underside grille, a greasy grime band, an amber glowing lamp strip underneath, and a rectangular duct rising to the ceiling at y 2.55 with clamp bands and rivets. Ceiling: five steelDark I-beams across x at y 2.45..2.55 (z -1.6, -0.8, 0, 0.8, 1.6), rib bars along z, and four recessed flat lamp panels (panelCream frames with an amber/cream glowing face) between the beams. A pipe bundle (pipeBundle, x -0.9, y 2.4) of four parallel tubes (orangePipe, copper, steel, hullGrey) along z -1.8..1.0 with flanges, valve wheels (red, small) and drip stains. A hanging utensil rail at utensilRail (y 1.6, z -1.72, x -0.9..1.7): a steel tube with ladles, spatulas, a whisk and a hanging pan with a cast-iron look (blackRubber) and hook rings. Two wall shelves above the sink (y 1.4 and 1.8, x -0.7..0.1) carrying jars and cans (rust, foodGreen, steel) with stencil labels. A swing-arm CRT monitor on the right wall (monitorArm at x -1.7, y 1.75): an articulated steel arm of three segments and a boxy hullGrey CRT housing with a black bezel, a glowing greenCRT screen with scanline bars and a tiny text-line blocks and a red power LED. A ceiling-mounted yellow rotating warning beacon in the front-left (x 1.5, z 0.2, y 2.35) with a cage. An intercom panel on the back wall at x 1.5, y 1.6 with a speaker grille (small parallel bars) and a cyanLed button. A ventilation grille at x -0.2, y 2.3 on the back wall (slatted steelDark). Its parts stay above y 1.45, except the shelves, rail and arm, which are fixed to wall faces.
parts.attaches: Wall fittings seat on backWallFace (z = -1.8) and rightWallFace (x = -1.8). The hood sits above the back run's range at hoodBase, with its underside at y 1.65, 0.7 m above the counter top. Ceiling beams and the duct reach the ceilingUnder level (y 2.5..2.6). It floats above the floor; nothing touches y = 0.

calls.reasoning:
I'm thinking through a prop group for an Alien Nostromo-style galley kitchen, deciding to keep it static with no joints for simplicity, and sketching out room dimensions and layout with counters along the walls.

I'm breaking the scene into parts: a floor deck and back bulkhead shell, a back wall with stove/hood and sink, a side wall with fridge and storage, a central mess table with benches and tableware, and an overhead layer of pipes, rails, and warning details to add Nostromo-style grime and clutter.

I'll split the scene into five roughly equal-budget parts, working out the overall shell dimensions, ceiling height, and deck thickness, then pinning down exact coordinates for the back counter and wall positions so everything aligns within the enclosing box.

Now I'm working out how the back counter and right-wall runs meet at the corner, dividing up which x/z ranges each part owns so there's no overlap and a doorway gap is left open on the left side.

For contents, I'm placing base cabinets, countertop, a 4-burner range with overhead hood, sink and faucet, microwave, and a coffee machine with glowing indicators along the back run, while the right run gets a tall fridge, cold storage lockers, freezer drawers, a dispenser with glowing display, and base counter storage.

Now I'm laying out the central mess table with bolted benches on either side, set within a bounded box that stays clear of the right run, and scattering trays, mugs, bowls, cutlery, sauce bottles, fruit, and food tins across its surface.

For the overhead zone, I'm placing ceiling lamp panels, a range hood with exhaust duct, a hanging utensil rail with pots along the back wall, shelves above the sink, an overhead pipe bundle, a swing-arm monitor, a warning light, hazard signage, and a ventilation grille, all bounded within the upper ceiling box and considering whether ceiling beams belong here too.

Now for the shell layer: deck grating, back and right wall panels, a doorway, baseboard conduits, floor hazard stripes, wall number stencils, and wall ribbing rising to the ceiling height. Since the shell forms the enclosure its box naturally overlaps everything else, which is fine, but I need to keep the wall panels at the inner face so mounted items like shelves and rails at the back wall don't collide with the plain shell geometry, and I'm working out where the doorway wall sits relative to the right-side x-range.

I'm picking a gritty Nostromo-style palette -- grimy beige and grey-green plastics, dull steel, amber CRT glow, hazard orange and yellow, dark charcoal rubber, faded cream panels, worn olive tones -- to color the hull, walls, deck, grating, and warning stripes.

Now I'm laying out key mount positions: deck, counter, and table heights, back/right wall and ceiling planes, door location, plus centers for the range, sink, and fridge fixtures.

I'm working out the right-side counter run's extents, figuring the fridge sits in the corner facing outward while the rest of the run holds the dispenser, drawers, and trash compactor, keeping depths and x-ranges consistent so nothing overlaps.

Now I'm budgeting part counts across sections—shell, back run, right run, table, overhead—keeping the total manageable, and noting style conventions: flat-colored parts, small stenciled label pieces, and glow kits reserved for indicator lights. Then I'll move to writing out the final JSON structure.

I need to write a function that builds the mess table, accepting a context object with destructured fields. Since the Ctx type isn't explicitly imported, I'll define my own local type for it to stay safe against typecheck issues rather than assuming it's global.

With no joints defined in the shared builder, parts without a bone reference will just stay in model space, so I'll use helper functions like box and cyl for geometry placement along with a glow kit import for screen elements. For colors, I'll reference the palette object directly by name, like P.hullGrey, P.steel, P.rust, and similar entries for the various materials.

Now I'm working out the table dimensions — slab thickness, top height, edge rim details, pedestal supports with foot flanges and bolt cylinders, figuring out exact coordinates for each component to build the physical structure piece by piece.

Moving on to the bench: positioning it at seat height 0.46 with a cream seat pad over a steel base plate, sizing the dimensions to roughly match the table's scale so the furniture set feels proportional.

I'm adding surface details like seam strips, wear patches, and rivets on the table and bench, but need to stay within my part budget of 170. To afford these small details I'm planning to merge geometries by color into a single part per color group, since the rule allows one part per bone and color combination.

Setting up the merge bucket system...

Still defining box/cylinder/sphere helpers and laying out table slab, rim, and leg positions using these coordinate placements...

Working out the slanted bar geometry...

Placing rivets along the inside rows and rim at regular z intervals, then adding a worn centre strip with subtle grime streaks layered slightly above it to avoid z-fighting.

Now I'm thickening the top slab to 0.08 units with a darker steel apron beneath it for a sturdier look, then placing two pedestal supports at specific z positions with a flange detail at their base to anchor them to the ground.

Adding more pedestal details...

Now I'm laying out the table placement, adding a center stretcher beam with bolts connecting the two pedestals, then planning the tableware arrangement on top—working out positions and sizes for food trays along each side of the table.

Each tray gets a steel base box with raised rim walls and internal dividers creating three compartments, holding flattened blob shapes for green and red food items, with mirrored compartment layouts for trays on the opposite side.

Now I'm detailing the fork and spoon utensils: thin steel handles with small heads, the fork having tiny tine boxes and the spoon having a flattened oval sphere for its bowl, varying food contents and occasionally leaving a tray with fewer items for variety.

I'm working out the exact placement of the utensils beside each tray, fitting them in the narrow gap between the tray edge and the table rim, and adjusting the rivet positions so they don't overlap with the forks and spoons.

Now I'm setting up the mug geometries for the center strip, using a cylinder for each mug body and a small arced torus to form the handle loop.

Adding the pitcher, salt and pepper shakers, and sauce bottle now—steel-blue tapered pitcher with handle and lip, cylindrical shakers with contrasting caps, and a dark red-brown sauce bottle with a narrow neck and red cap.

I'm placing a folded napkin box with an offset fold line, a dropped spoon resting on the floor near the table, and a half-eaten food tin with a steel body, greenish interior disc, and a partially open lid.

Now I'm designing a data-pad prop: a steel body with a rubber bezel and glowing green CRT screen, dark text bars and small amber/red button lights, positioned at a slight tilt on the table, plus some flat grime smear discs scattered around.

Next I'm placing a coffee spill with a stained disc and tiny droplets, plus a ring mark on the table. Then I'm laying out the center strip objects — pitcher, and three mugs positioned around the table and bench seat, adjusting rotations so handles face outward.

I continue refining positions: a fourth mug near the top, salt and pepper shakers spaced closely with small radii, the sauce bottle shifted lower, and a napkin angled near a tin container, keeping everything within the tray's bounds.

Checking hazard stripes and tray zones along the z-axis for the second scene to make sure the mug, pitcher, and tray don't overlap—then I start placing a data-pad object.

I move it slightly to avoid collisions with mug B, settling on coordinates (0.02, 0.28) with a size around 0.11x0.16, and adjust mug B's position to (-0.085, 0.28) to keep clearance tight but acceptable given its handle orientation. I then start positioning mug A at (0.085, -0.12), orienting its handle outward.

I'm placing the napkin near the tin on the table, keeping both within safe gaps between trays. Then I'm figuring out bench item placement—maybe a mug or dropped spoon on the bench seats, making sure each item sits properly on the table top or bench surface.

I'm also working out the bench seat's worn texture details, like darker grime stripes and small tufting buttons placed at regular intervals, plus adding a tiny stenciled number plate to the bench base for a worn, hazard-marked look.

Now I'm building a reusable helper for drawing seven-segment digit displays out of small boxes, so I can stamp plate numbers like "03" onto the pedestal front faces and bench ends, deciding which faces are actually visible given the cabinet's open front.

I'm also adding small details like hazard stripes near table feet, grime strips on bench legs, bolt heads and rivets along the rubber strip edges, and leg brackets at the bench frame span.

Now I'm working out the bench leg frame geometry itself — leg boxes, foot plates, cross braces, and diagonal X-braces connecting them at the proper positions and spans.

Placing bracket plates, then working out the bench geometry for both sides: seat pads, base plates, legs, and rubber edge strips, aligning their heights and positions so everything stacks correctly from ground to seat level.

Skipping that detail. Adding grime patches and rust streaks on the seat and pedestal for wear, then writing the tray function with its base box and side walls.

Now I'm working out the tray's internal layout using local coordinates flipped by x, placing dividers to split the big compartment from the smaller ones, and positioning the contents (a scaled sphere, a small box, and another scaled sphere) with color variants inside each section.

Writing utensil generation code...

Still writing the geometry helpers...

I'm grouping geometries by color and glow, then merging each bucket at the end with mergeGeometries from BufferGeometryUtils and adding them as parts at the origin, applying glow where needed. Since there are no joints defined, I'll skip bone assignment and just rely on the root. All the shapes use indexed position/normal/uv attributes so merging should work cleanly, and I'm using flat shading to recompute normals after the merge.

I'm checking the color budget against the shared 64-color palette, picking a small set of my own colors (coffee, pitcher blue, worn pad) alongside foodRed and grime for accents, keeping it to just a few extras. I'm also planning glow intensities for the CRT green screen and small amber/red LEDs, then starting to write the seven-segment digit rendering logic facing forward.

Now I'm positioning the number plates on the pedestal face and designing a hazard warning label for the side faces—yellow plate with black top/bottom strips and a small warning triangle, using a sub-context helper function to rotate it to face outward on either x side.

I'm simplifying the warning symbol to a black bar and dot forming an exclamation mark, rotating a cylinder so its axis aligns with the facing direction. I'm also adding grime streaks and rust drips on the pedestal, then writing a reusable hazard-stripe function that builds a yellow base strip with black diagonal bars for the table edges.

Working out z-fighting between the hazard bars and the base slab by nudging heights slightly, spacing seventeen bars evenly while skipping the ends, and adding a worn steel center strip with randomized grime streaks for extra realism.

Now I'm scaling that scuff randomization and designing a data-pad prop — a dark steel body with a black rubber bezel and a glowing green CRT-style screen, stacking their heights carefully so they layer correctly on top of each other.

Then I sketch dark bars across the screen to suggest lines of text, plus small amber buttons and a red LED indicator for detail. After that I move on to a tin prop: a steel cylinder body with a food-red label band and a steel rim on top.

For the tin's contents, I add a disc of food-colored material with a bite taken out, then work out the lid geometry—positioning it tilted and hinged at the back edge, calculating the hinge pivot and rotated center so it looks like it's propped open from one side.

Now I'm starting to define a mug function with parameters for substance, color, and handle orientation, beginning with a tapered cylinder body for the mug shape.

Adding pitcher details...

Adding a small stain disc on the napkin, then flattening spheres via non-uniform scaling to fake grime smears and a coffee drop near the edge, positioned just barely poking above the table surface.

Now I'm placing a dropped spoon on the floor, working out a spot that fits in the narrow gap between the bench and table without overlapping either, settling on x=0.6, z=0.35, oriented along z.

Floor pieces rest at the deck top height (y=0.08) rather than y=0, since the deck slab occupies that base layer. I'm adding bench foot plates around y=0.085, plus small hex bolt cylinders on the plate corners for detail, and planning similar floor bolts for the table pedestal.

Adding flange bolts and washers...

I'll skip extra hazard striping to avoid overcomplicating the pedestal, but I'm adding steel corner reinforcement plates with rivets at the four top corners of the table slab, and considering thin grime streaks along the slab's side edges for added realism.

Now I'm placing a small stenciled label plate ("MESS 1"-style digits) on the slab's front face near z=0.9, positioning the digit plate and rim end strips carefully so everything aligns with the slab's front edge.

I need to nudge the rim slightly outward from the slab's side faces to avoid z-fighting — widening the rim strips to 0.024 centered around ±0.542 so the outer edge sits at 0.554, and adjusting the end strips similarly around z=0.892.

Then I'm adjusting the rim's vertical placement so its bottom aligns coplanar with the slab's bottom at 0.695, height 0.09, with the apron sitting right below it touching the pedestal top at 0.67, and placing small rivet cylinders along the rim top at y=0.786.

Now I'm positioning the hazard stripes at both ends, checking that each stripe's depth keeps it clear of the rim's inner face, and verifying the tray, mug, and pitcher placements don't collide with the stripes given their respective z-offsets and radii. I'm also sizing a scuffed wear strip down the center, roughly 0.3 wide.

I'm settling on a worn-steel color for the strip with patches of grime overlaid, since it should read as both metal-exposed wear and dirt buildup. After a quick triangle budget check to confirm I'm well under the limit, I'm moving on to writing the bench geometry, setting up center positions and lengths for each one.

Placing the base plate, cushioned pad, and rubber edge strips...

Adding leg frames and foot plates...

Adding grime and rust detailing to the legs and feet, then moving to the pedestal structure — defining its main body box, flange, and positioning per face with numbered labels for each pedestal.

Adding more ribs, then placing an access plate with rivets and a handle, a number plate with digits, and side hazard labels on the faces.

Now I'm setting up grime streaks and rust drips via randomized thin boxes, plus a grime band near the pedestal-to-top joint.

Starting the implementation code, importing three.js utilities and geometry merging helpers to build out the mesh structure.

Defining the function signature for the mess table builder, working out which fields to destructure from context and skipping unused ones to keep typechecking clean. Working out the floor and table top coordinates from the mount metadata to position elements correctly.

I'll just go with literal values matching the defaults rather than deriving everything from M, setting up the color palette object and confirming the rng function usage for scatter placement. Now I'm starting the put implementation with a bucket map for spatial grouping.

Writing geometry placement logic...

Still writing geometry helpers...

Still writing digit segment helper...

Adding rim end caps and rivets...

Adding scuff marks and grime streaks with randomized positions, sizes, and rotations along the worn strip and slab sides, alternating between grime and steel-dark colors for variation.

Still writing scene details... now moving on to defining a tray-building function that places items on trays with mirrored positions based on which side of the bench they're on.

Still placing contents and color variants...

For eaten-food variants I'm swapping the big blob for crumbs instead, and adding a small grime smudge on the tray base. Then I'm positioning utensils along the tray edge, alternating fork and spoon, sized to fit within the rim.

Still writing utensil geometry...

Working out the pedestal face transforms, using local offsets with rotation about y by ±π/2 to map local z onto world x for the side faces, and setting up the type alias for the builder function's return type.

Since the return type is self-referential, I realize the implicit recursive type will cause a TS error, so I need to define an explicit interface for the builder object with its box, cyl, sph, tor, and sub methods, where sub itself returns that same interface. Defining interface now...

I'm defining buildBackRun using the shared Ctx type, placing parts without bones at the root since there are no joints defined for this static model.

I'm setting up helper functions for boxes and cylinders (centered, ranged, and directional variants with axis-aligned orientation) to build the counter geometry — a kick plate, steel cabinet body, and stainless countertop slab spanning the front-to-back depth, all using a flat color palette with glow accents on amber and cyan elements. Now I'm laying out the cabinet segments along the x-axis starting from the prep station.

Still planning fixture placement...

Coffee machine goes at x 1.22..1.46, with counter ending near x 1.75 and a bulkhead end panel at 1.85. I'm separating the range top as its own stainless slab from x 0.2..1.2, with counter slabs flanking it on either side, and now working out how to build the sink area by placing basin pieces around the recess rather than cutting a hole in the slab.

Since the cabinet body under the sink would otherwise poke up through the basin cavity, I'm lowering that section's cabinet top so the basin walls and dark recessed floor can sit properly inside without clipping through the countertop.

For colors I'll use the palette P.* entries alongside custom ones, and I'll apply the glow helper from the kit where appropriate. I need to stay mindful of the 190 part budget, so I'll keep that in mind without necessarily merging same-color pieces.

For the rivets, I'm planning to merge each row into a single part using mergeGeometries from BufferGeometryUtils, building small rotated cylinders and combining them to save on part count while keeping consistent indexed geometry.

For the smaller details like scuffs and label strips, I'm setting up a bucket system that accumulates translated box geometries per color and flushes them into merged parts at the end, keeping flat shading and matching attributes so everything merges cleanly within the triangle budget.

I'll keep mostly palette colors with maybe one or two extras, and handle glow separately with its own bucket keyed by color and glow strength so emissive parts merge independently from regular geometry.

Writing bucket helper code...

Still defining geometry helpers...

Then for flushing I'll merge each bucket's geometries and attach them as single flat-shaded parts positioned near the origin since there are no bones to anchor to.

Now I'm laying out cabinet coordinates: a steel-dark body box spanning the kickspace to top height, with steel door panels layered slightly in front and inset with small gaps so the dark body shows through as seam lines.

Still defining sink geometry...

I'm working out the basin interior: a stainless floor sunk below the opening with thin side walls going down from the slab surface, plus a darker recessed drain disc at the bottom for contrast. Since the slab itself defines the opening edges, the basin walls essentially extend from the slab's cut edges down to the floor, so I don't need separate wall geometry beyond that.

Now I'm laying out the actual slab segments as individual boxes - a left counter piece over the prep area, then the sink section broken into front and back strips plus narrow edge strips between and around the basin cutouts, sized to leave the openings clear.

For the range section, x 0.2..1.2, I'm deciding on a stainless top plate at y 0.87..0.95 with a slightly raised lip from 0.95 to 0.975, keeping it visually consistent with the counter height while leaving room for burner grates to sit on top.

Now I'm adding a stainless backsplash lip running along the back edge at z -1.78..-1.74 across the full counter width including the range area, plus working out the front slab edge and door panel positions so they stay flush near z -1.1 to -1.115.

I'm placing a recessed black rubber kick plate along the base, slightly inset from the front face, and adding subtle grime streaks for realism, with the deck resting at y 0.08. For the prep section doors, I'm defining a door panel spanning roughly x -1.09 to -0.61 with a drawer above it, and starting a helper function to generate door panels consistently across the cabinet run.

Still adjusting door panel depths...

Sink section splits into two doors flanking a steel fascia panel with label strips up top. Range gets an oven door with steel frame and window spanning the center-right, topped by a control panel plate with knobs across the upper band.

For the oven door window, I'm adding a dark glass panel with a thin amber glow strip along the bottom edge to suggest a light inside. I'm debating the handle geometry — letting it protrude slightly beyond the bounding box since it's a chunky prop detail, deciding small overshoots up to about 0.04 are acceptable for knobs and handles rather than reworking the door depth.

Moving to the right side, I'm laying out three stacked drawers each with their own handle, plus a thin end cap strip to close off the body edge at x 1.75.
